title: Periodic-Pulse Control of Collective Emission and Photon Statistics in Interacting Quantum Emitters
authors: Kavalambramalil George Paulson, Fu Li, Hanna Terletska
abstract: We investigate the collective emission spectra and photon correlations of two identical dipole-dipole-coupled emitters under continuous-wave (CW) and periodic pulsed driving. Our results show that a periodic train of instantaneous $π_x$ pulses can generate emission spectra whose dominant features closely resemble those obtained under CW excitation. We find that the structure of the collective emission spectra reflects the interplay among the resonance conditions, dipole-dipole coupling, and the inter-pulse delay $τ_D$. We further demonstrate that finite-duration $π_x$ pulses with sufficiently high Rabi frequencies can closely reproduce the ideal instantaneous-pulse limit. In contrast to the emission spectra, the photon correlations $g^{(2)}(t,τ)$ are governed primarily by $τ_D$ and, unlike under CW driving, become increasingly insensitive to the resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit. These results establish periodic pulsed driving as a versatile means of tailoring both the emission spectra and the photon statistics of coupled two-emitter systems.
summary: This paper explores controlling the light emitted by two coupled quantum emitters using periodic laser pulses. It demonstrates that pulsing allows for independent control over the emission spectrum and the photon statistics. This capability makes pulsed driving a powerful tool for tailoring quantum light sources compared to steady-state continuous driving.
main_problem: The study investigates how periodic pulsed driving can control the collective emission spectra and photon statistics of two interacting quantum emitters, comparing this to continuous-wave (CW) excitation.
main_result: Periodic pulsed driving offers a versatile control mechanism, allowing the photon statistics ($g^{(2)}$) to become insensitive to resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit, while the emission spectrum is still tunable by the inter-pulse delay ($	au_D$).
method: The analysis uses the master equation formalism to model the time evolution of the two-emitter system under both CW and pulsed driving protocols.
model_or_system: The system consists of two identical, dipole-dipole-coupled two-level emitters. The dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian and a master equation incorporating collective decay and coupling strengths.
key_observables: Collective emission spectra and the two-time photon correlation function, $g^{(2)}(t, 	au)$.
important_parameters: Inter-pulse delay ($	au_D$), Rabi frequency ($\Omega$), and detuning ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Born-Markov approximation and often utilizes the instantaneous-pulse limit approximation for pulsed driving.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level diagrams, the dependence of $g^{(2)}(t, 	au)$ on $	au_D$ for pulsed driving, and comparisons of $g^{(2)}$ under CW versus pulsed driving at different resonance conditions.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the Hamiltonian and master equation, then analyzes the spectral properties under CW driving, and finally extends the analysis to periodic pulsed driving to compare the control capabilities over spectra and photon statistics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum control in open quantum systems, showing how time-domain engineering (pulsing) can decouple spectral control from photon statistics control, which is highly relevant for designing quantum light sources.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Energy level diagrams of an identical two-emitter system in the bare, collective, and dressed bases are shown in Figs(a), (b), and (c), respectively.

FIG. 2. Collective emission spectrum from a coupled two identical (∆1 = ∆2) emitter system under continuous driv- ing fields for ˆµ ⊥ˆr12. In (a) and (b), the laser is tuned to two-photon resonance (2ω0 = 2ωL) with Rabi frequencies Γ and 30Γ, respectively. The laser is tuned to the transition frequency of the superradiant state (∆= −Ω12) in (c) and (d), with the Rabi frequency set to Γ and 30Γ, respectively. The cases of weak and strong dipole–dipole coupling are con- sidered, corresponding to r12 = λ/4 and r12 = λ/20, where r12 and λ denote the interatomic distance and the resonant wavelength, respectively. The total time of evolution is con- sidered to be Γt = 4.

FIG. 3. Normalized spectral distance ˜DS, tracking the rela- tive change between spectra at successive times, for a con- tinuously driven system of two identical coupled emitters (∆1 = ∆2) with ˆµ ⊥ˆr12. Panels (a) and (b) correspond to two-photon resonance (2ωL = 2ω0) at Rabi frequencies Γ and 30Γ, respectively, while panels (c) and (d) correspond to driving at the superradiant transition frequency (∆= −Ω12), at Rabi frequencies Γ and 30Γ, respectively. In each case, re- sults are shown for weak (r12 = λ/4) and strong (r12 = λ/20) dipole-dipole coupling, where r12 is the interatomic separa- tion and λ is the resonant wavelength.

FIG. 4. Collective emission spectrum from a coupled two identical (∆1 = ∆2) emitter system under global σx rota- tion for ˆµ ⊥ˆr12. In (a) and (b), the laser is tuned to two- photon resonance (2ω0 = 2ωL), and in (c) and (d), the laser is tuned to the transition frequency of the superradiant state (∆= −Ω12). The rotation around the x axis is performed at inter pulse intervals τ = 0.1, 0.5 and 2.0 for dipole-dipole cou- pling strengths corresponding to r12 = λ/4 and r12 = λ/20, respectively. r12 and λ denote the interatomic distance and the resonant wavelength, respectively. The total time of evo- lution is considered to be Γt = 4.

FIG. 5. (a) Gate error, 1−Fg, for a finite-duration π pulse as a function of the pulse Rabi frequency Ω0/Γ and the dipole-dipole coupling strength Ω12/Γ. The gate error decreases as Ω0 increases, indicating that suﬀiciently strong finite-duration pulses closely approximate the ideal instantaneous σx rotation, even in the presence of inter-emitter coupling. (b) Spectral distance, SD, between the spectra generated by finite-duration and instantaneous pulse sequences, evaluated for Np = 10 pulses. Smaller values of SD indicate better agreement with the instantaneous-pulse limit.
